regenerable_on: any guest running paperless-ngx with its API reachable and a token belonging to a user with global visibility, staged as harness/bin/se-capture-guest's paperless case expects: SE_PAPERLESS_URL and SE_PAPERLESS_TOKEN in the capturing environment, forwarded to the guest and sent as the Authorization header. The archive must be NON-EMPTY and must define at least one tag, one correspondent, one document type and one inbox tag, or five of the fourteen facts below go absent and the capture stops discriminating a working port from one that publishes nothing. Three plain-text documents are enough; paperless parses text/plain natively, so no OCR stack is needed. The version string moves with the image, so a re-stage re-reads the anchors by hand in the same change.
anonymisation_note: Through BOTH halves of the gate, and no substitution was needed — the manifest-driven run reported zero, and the independent detectors, which share no pattern or code path with it, found nothing. That is a property of what this variant IS rather than luck: paperless was stood up in a disposable lab VM, its three documents are invented lab prose written by the capture itself, and every leaf in the status document is a build constant or the app's self-check. harness/scrub/paperless.json states the one bound that matters and states it loudly — `database.url` and `tasks.redis_url` are `nothing` HERE because they hold a container-internal sqlite path and a docker service name, and a paperless on Postgres or a remote broker writes CREDENTIALS into both, which must be refused rather than substituted.
note:
The product's first CREDENTIALED adapter, captured. One instance, two documents, ONE row — `/api/statistics/` and `/api/status/` are separate requests feeding a single object, so a port that published a row per document gets a different commit count from the same payloads.

What this variant is FOR is the count. The subsystem exists because of two incidents with one shape — a healthy container row over a broken archive, once when a secret drift emptied the library 38 -> 0 — and DocumentCount is the fact both needed surfaced. So the archive here is deliberately non-empty and deliberately varied: three documents, two tags, one correspondent, one document type, one of the three filed to the inbox. All five inventory facts are therefore VALUES, and a port that dropped any of them prints red rather than reproducing a plausible-looking subset.

The classifier is the second thing this variant teaches. `classifier_status` is WARNING with `classifier_error` 'No classifier training tasks found', which is the app being HONEST about a young archive and not a fault — the glossary says so in as many words. A capture from a mature archive reports OK there and exercises neither the WARNING word nor the error text, so this young-archive state is the more informative one and is why the variant was staged before any training ran.

Stated bounds, because a specimen shows one instance on one day.

The token belonged to a superuser, so the counts are the archive's. /api/statistics/ is PERMISSION-SCOPED — a low-privilege token sees 0 documents in an archive of 38 and nothing in the response says so — and that failure is the exact incident this subsystem exists to catch. No committed capture stages it, because staging it means capturing a document whose numbers are a LIE about the archive, and the honest place to catch it is a second variant with a narrowed token. It does not exist yet.

/api/status/ answered, because the token was admin. A token without that grant turns the component checks into StatusUnobservable with the HTTP reason and leaves the inventory numbers standing — a different row shape, and this capture reaches none of it.

No failure path is exercised at all: the API answered both paths. A missing SE_PAPERLESS_URL (the decline that retires), a token that cannot survive a header (the newline-paste refusal the adapter makes at construction), and a configured instance whose API is dark are three statements this collector must make and no committed capture stages any of them.

The row carries values only — no names family, no absent list, no unobservable record, no relation assertion. paperless publishes no identifier that survives a rename; the object's native name is the constant `paperless`, so law 1 has nothing here to carry.

Sqlite, not Postgres, and a co-located redis. Both are the compose defaults and both are why the two connection URLs are harmless in this capture; see the manifest's bound.
anchors_note:
Read off payloads/api-statistics.json and payloads/api-status.json by hand at staging, before any stream existed, which is what makes them an authority the reference-generated half is not.

The object is named `paperless` because that is the row's NATIVE name; the id the adapter mints is `instance:paperless` and the collator derives it from the declared prefix and this name, so an anchor on the id would assert the collator's work rather than the collector's.

The five inventory anchors are five DIFFERENT numbers on purpose — 3, 1, 2, 1, 1. A port that transposed two of the five members would still satisfy an anchor set where every count was 1, and this collection's whole value is that the numbers are right. DocumentCount 3 and InboxCount 1 in particular can only be transposed with each other in a document whose members sit adjacent.

The four `*_error` absences are the half a value anchor cannot state, and they discriminate the exact spelling a port is likely to reach for. The document PRESENTS all four members holding JSON `null`; the reference publishes an error fact only `if tasks.get(member)` and `if database.get('error')`, so a port that published a fact whenever the key existed emits four facts of null — which the contract's fact_value refuses and which is the same defect traefik's noop@internal anchors catch. Anchoring the absence rather than a value is what makes a regression to null print red, since an anchor asserting null would be asserting the unassertable.

ClassifierError is anchored as a VALUE beside those four absences precisely because it is the one that IS populated. The pair separates 'the port omits error keys correctly' from 'the port omits error keys always' — a port blind to the whole error channel satisfies four anchors and fails this one.

StatusUnobservable is absent because /api/status/ answered. It is the one fact whose PRESENCE would mean the collection is reporting a failure rather than a reading, so it is anchored absent for the same reason the commit count is: a port that fell into its narrowed arm on every run would still emit a row and still commit one object.

StorageTotalBytes and StorageAvailableBytes are anchored as exact integers, not because the numbers matter, but because they are the two largest values in the capture and both exceed 2^32. A port that decoded them through a float32, or that published them as strings, fails here where an eyeball comparing 'about 63 GB' would not.

commit_objects 1 is anchored because absence is not the only way to lose a collection: a port that emitted one row per DOCUMENT satisfies every fact anchor above and reports 2 here.

Deliberately NOT anchored: `sanity_check_status` and `llmindex_status`. Both are present in the payload, both carry a status word, and the reference publishes NEITHER — its tuple names redis, celery, index and classifier and no others. Anchoring them would assert facts this collection does not publish; leaving them unanchored while they sit in the payload is what makes the next reader check the tuple rather than assume every `*_status` member becomes a fact. `install_type`, `server_os`, `database.type`, `latest_migration` and the whole `tasks.summary` block are unanchored for the same reason — in the payload, reaching no row, because a fact must be cited by an opinion, used in identity or a relation, or be part of the declared answer (DESIGN 15).
